articles.title: Trump Signs Order to Reduce Childhood Vaccines, Repeats Unfounded Autism Link
articles.summary: It is unusual, if not unprecedented, for detailed vaccine policy to emerge from the White House.

comments.name: Paul Brown
comments.body:
It’s maddening that the media slavishly repeat the charge that the President or Mr. Kennedy link “childhood shots and autism—a connection that scientists have said is unfounded.” That’s what scientists say. It’s not what scientists have proven conclusively. Readers deserve both sides of the story until and unless scientists can prove the case one way or the other. 

Also, I am puzzled that medical groups express surprise and seeming outrage that the Administration wants “to scale back childhood vaccines in a bid to explore an alleged connection to autism.” Until established science can explain the scary increase in the incidence of autism in the United States, why oppose so violently an attempt to explore? I suspect that the outrage is more an attempt to disparage the President than it is to help medically children who may be suffering.

Nor does it mention anything about autism as a predicate for the Order.  The President's opinion--however (yet) unsubstantiated--is his opinion. As with the government's malfeasant response to Covid, its policy on childhood vaccination doesn't occur in a vacuum: dozens of advanced, scientifically proficient, democratic countries throughout Europe and elsewhere have chosen to rely on education and choice rather than mandates to ensure broad vaccination, childhood immunity, and parental trust among their populations. New mutations often emerge from the swamp. But one of our most enduring ancient biases is that the good, better radiates down from up high to bring new and improved changes into our world. But it seems often the case that the new and improved develops down low and rises upward. The Darwinian view: from the simple to the more complex, as the old complex fails, the simple has the chance to develop into the new complexity.

In other words, our seeming fracturing, atomization, decadence, our foul seediness (Hamlet: "Fie on't! ah, fie! 'tis an unweeded garden, / That grows to seed; things rank and gross in nature / Possess it merely.") is also producing the seeds and mutations of the new, as an unweeded garden does — the new and improved of the future.

Many of our old ways, our beliefs and habits, deserve to be broken apart and replaced. Breaking up of various sorts can be hard, painful, full of anguish. But it also opens space, makes opportunities for what may eventually prove to be the better. The dying of the big dinosaurs brought about the flourishing of the little mammals, the opening of Pandora's box released new forces, out of chaos comes the new order.

comments.name: Norma
comments.body: A further thought prompted by the Jason Arday debacle at my alma mater, Cambridge University:  Last year, a small group of female undergraduates founded the Cambridge University Society of Women, in support of women's rights and the right to single-sex association.  In response, certain of their fellow students subjected these young women to personal threats, vitriolic online abuse, and a targeted petition demanding their outright ban. These brave women persisted, demonstrating great personal courage, and the CUSW continues to flourish.  In complete contrast, while these women students, exercising their legal and human rights, were left to navigate a hostile environment, the university hierarchy actively shielded Jason Arday from credible allegations of plagiarism and credential fabrication, dismissing any investigation as a vile smear campaign and enabling police action against the journalist who exposed him. This stark juxtaposition—where female students of high intelligence and impeccable integrity were abandoned to the vicious hostility of a fashionable ideology, while a male academic (whose ill-written, garbage-stuffed PhD thesis I have read with horror) was protected from serious misconduct charges—exposes a systemic rot that pervades this and other institutions and compromises their moral and academic integrity.

People who have neither money, privilege, glamour, or hunkiness, just hearts capable of being touched, devotion,  persistence and striving to improve themselves and their relationship, and make something beautiful of what they have and the person and family they have made their life with.

I am under no illusion that it would ever see the light of day, though Lord knows there is room for something less formulaic than a Hallmark romance movie -or greeting card.  

The best selling work of fiction in the English language is probably Jane Austin’s Pride and Prejudice, which was published when romances were equally formulaic, and even more well mannered.  Austin takes a verbal rapier and slices the lady’s dropped handkerchief in two before it hits the ground.  Lizzy is a girl on the cusp of adulthood who shares some of the values of the time, but is steadfast in her values and fearless rather than submissive.  Her confrontation with the imperious Lady Catherine de Bourgh is on the short list for greatest verbal duels in the English Language.

Romances these days aspire to that kind of success.  They may write spunky, sharp-tongued heroines.  But there is little risk of inspired writing or being challenged by Hallmark.

But sometimes when you are tired of the struggle, you want to curl up until the happily ever after.

comments.name: Barbara

The intensity of the shirtwaist fad was already starting to fade in 1912, leading the Triangle factory owners to cut costs as sales declined. One way was to lock the girls in to prevent theft — they were inspected at the end of the workday. They also eliminates the time allotted for basic maintenance like sweeping up and disposing of highly flammable scraps and remnants.

comments.body: I've never been to Afghanistan, but this haunts me too. How would it feel to be free, and then to have it all snatched away and live life as if I were a slave or POW? It's the worst for the women who were once free. I imagine subsequent generations will feel more comfortable in their horrible situations as the memory of freedom disappears as their mothers and granothers die off, and the repressive culture robs them of even enough education to understand what they've lost, or what they could be. But that makes me even angrier, and sadder. One day, the great grand children of free, independent women will very likely defend their repressive government, shake their fists at Western culture, burn flags, and inform on other women who break repressive Taliban rules. Some will even patrol the streets with whips or guns to make sure their sisters do as they're told.

The primary goal was to capture or kill Osama bin Laden and those who plotted with him to attack the US.  We did this with the help of a lot of good Afghanis who should have been relocated to the US as promised, but it is fortunate that at least some portion of such people and others like Mursal were able to come here and thrive.  I think she should be more grateful about that and much less recriminating about what was inevitable by the Taliban despite the best efforts of the US, not because we failed to sacrifice on their behalf indefinitely.

comments.name: Steve Vining
comments.body: Immigration crack downs in the US are cyclical and typically occur after surges in immigration creates unrest with the native population.  The US is a country of immigrants and immigrants have helped create the dynamism of the American economy which is the envy of the world.  The current anti-immigrant anger will fade in time when the economic impacts of a declining population start to impact the economy.  Automation can help with some things, but robots aren't going to buy your house or your used car when you want to sell it and as the law of supply and demand work, people will demand we get the population growing again even if it means increased immigration.  When immigration laws are reformed, as they eventually will be, they need to focus on getting the best and brightest to come here to start businesses and raise their families.

comments.name: Brett D
comments.body:
You cannot have open borders and a welfare state as Milton Friedman declared decades ago. The number of people crossing the border in search of handouts will eventually bankrupt the nation.

If you want immigration then you have to stop the welfare. The message to the immigrants needs to be "if you want to come you, you better roll up your sleeves and work hard, because there will be no handouts".

comments.name: R Stockton
comments.body:
This specific political issue is fascinating because it seems that 30-40% of the population would cite opposition to current immigration patterns as a top political concern.

And then a similar figure of about 30% or so of the electorate on the other side believe that any changes, much less restrictions, to immigration are unthinkably un-American, xenophobic, and so on.  

As long as one side is sympathetic to, or simply likes, higher levels of immigration, it becomes very difficult for even close to a majority of the opposition to stop it.

Makes for quite the divisive issue on both sides of the Atlantic.

A particularly interesting aspect of European immigration is that many of these states were built around ethnic identity in a way that the U.S. as a country wasn't.  Many of the borders, as they are currently drawn, were fought over for centuries, often along ethnic lines.  I'd imagine that would make the immigration debate a bit different from one in a place like the U.S., which has had a long history of higher immigration levels than our Western European friends.

The test intentionally allowed internet access, disabled safeguards, and gave an agent a task; the system then pursued the task beyond the evaluators’ intended limits. AI systems can be misused, and high-risk deployments deserve targeted rules. From what I can see, it's the new Golden Calf, the false god that will lead us out of the desert to a land of abundance.  The term Superintelligence (and AGI) is meaningless - there's no clear definition by which one could establish whether you have "it", or not.  The one thing that we can comfortably say about Superintelligence is that, if your rival gets it before you, you're at a fatal disadvantage.  And so companies and countries are pouring unfathomable sums into making sure they don't get behind, and in the process creating new concentrations of wealth and power for a limited few.  Meanwhile, The current Sub-Superintelligence that we have today is doing a great job disrupting the world in ways that already have profound impact, and as the AGI-ers predict, we ain't seen nothin yet.  The truth is, we don't need AI to be any more super than it already is to see where it's all going.  But because we presumably haven't reached the point where AI becomes "super", the world is living in a state of frantic anticipation, lulled by a shocked acceptance of the seemingly inevitable future into kicking the can down the road - just like the frog that swims happily in the pot as the water slowly boils. comments.body: Such an incredible experience. We saw it in Ohio a couple years ago. That chasing shadow! We knew it was a shadow but it looked like a black wall coming at us. My fight or flight response kicked in and I wanted to RUN away from it.   The anxiety was real as it washed over us. Such a strange feeling. The eclipse itself was surreal. So glad we made the drive. We joined in and had no idea what was happening since we hadn't been reading the newspapers.  Was there a Nessie sighting, haha.  Then, we were stunned to watch the sun disappear completely.  I remember the temperature went dark and very cold, very quickly.  Then warmed up in matter of seconds. Such an eerie feeling.

comments.name: Buzzy
comments.body: Should we expect the sunset to appear meaningfully different if we're somewhere where the eclipse happens at sunset, and is partial (<40%)? I looked at the link, but it's hard to tell what's likely to be discernible with the naked eye. (Also -- the internet is very confusing on the topic of whether it's hazardous to look at sunsets directly, eclipse or no eclipse. Can we watch the partial eclipse sunset without equipment?)

comments.name: Ed
comments.body: I witnessed the 2024 eclipse in Austin, TX.  It was cloudy all morning, but sure enough, the clouds parted just in time for the eclipse to be fully visible.  It got dark very quickly, a very eerie feeling.  Maybe not pitch dark, but darker than dusk, I thought.  My little dog sat out in the yard with me and seemed rather amazed by everything.  My neighbors next door were shouting out from their yard.  The one thing I missed, but wished I could have seen, was the shadow of the moon racing across the earth as the sun was being completely covered.  The cloud cover prevented that.  It was quite an experience.

comments.name: Alan
comments.body: So many advantages in going electric. The reduction in air pollution was mentioned late in the article, but is perhaps the greatest benefit. People will live longer more enjoyable, healthier  lives. The reduction in noise is overlooked but another huge benefit. I live in Brooklyn, NY in an area where there are a lot of people riding very very loud motorcycles--it's deafening! The long term mechanical and maintenance costs are lower, like electric cars there are fewer parts to deal with, and will continue to drop as battery technology improves. This spring the bump in gas prices ticked me off so much I decided to add a scooter to my collection (a used Taiwanese 2018 Kymco 300cc gas model) with tons of underseat storage and a rear mounted "trunk box".  This has allowed me to leave my car parked sometimes for days at a time and I now run all my errands and commute to work on the scooter while enjoying 70MPG.  If electric models become widely available I would consider upgrading.  By Labor Day I expect to have clawed back nearly $1000 in gas savings (equivalent to half the price I paid for the Kymco).  Riding a scooter is actually extremely fun and the 70mph top speed allows for longer trips on 55mph 2-lane roads with ease.  It is a shame that so few scooters are offered for sale in the US which has been slow to embrace this form of transportation.

The rest of the world won't be far behind.  Of course YCC won't solve the actual debt problem, but it may help buy time while an actual solution is implemented. We probably still have a few years until we get to that point, probably early in the first term of the next president, at about the same time as the entitlement programs start to fail without support.  It won't be pretty but most likely it will get solved.  And the illusion of money not being a scarce thing, that began in 1971, went into overdrive after 2008, and went full-on insane during Covid, will come to an end.

comments.name: MA
comments.body:
Years ago, I worked briefly for a small-town weekly newspaper that had been around for decades.  My boss used to say, "what we publish is 'refrigerator news,'" by which he meant, stories and pictures that Grandma or Mom cuts out and hangs on the fridge with a magnet to enjoy and show everyone who comes into the house.  We published plenty of other stories, too, but no edition went out without the all-important local sports scores, graduation photos and focus on local life and issues. The small town I live in now has a similar paper. In a gone-crazy world, newsprint, ink and a sense of community are reassuring reminders that not all intelligence is artificial and controlled by people "from away." 
Wonder if the photo of Mr. Frost in his office with the tumbling stacks of papers reminded anyone else of the comic strip 'Shoe'?

comments.name: Susan F
comments.body:
I've worked for three family-owned newspapers and spent about 10 years in "community journalism," in the 1980s-90s. All three were sold to other companies when the next generation lost interest in the relatively unremunerative business--and that was before the Internet.
 It's very rewarding to feel you are making a difference, helping people understand issues like how proposed zoning and development affects them, the process of siting landfills and freeways, covering classrooms and school board meetings. 
This editor understands "names are news" and the importance of his readers knowing he's invested in them. 
Like teaching, local journalism is a labor of love, not something you do for the money. I used to joke with teachers I covered that education and journalism are about the two lowest-paid jobs requiring a college education, yet where would we be without these two professions?

comments.name: Paul Reale

That is a nice area, from Glens Falls to Lake George to Fort Ticonderoga.

comments.name: Roberto
comments.body:
It's a delicate balance to keep the advertisers happy enough to keep buying ads and to tell the community what it must know to be aware of any shady characters or developments in business and town/regional governance--so they can vote the responsible scoundrels out and jail any miscreants and fraudsters. And the "fluff" pieces city papers shun--the reports of schools' sports and other doings, community center programs, etc.--are what keep communities knitted together, and what keep people talking to one another. Anything to draw in younger readers is a huge plus. 

A community here took over one experienced journalist/editor's labor of love to create a community newspaper that would report the facts and has made it into a nonprofit. It supports citizen journalism and provides some internships for high school and college journalism students. So far, so good. I wish there were a paper edition every couple of weeks, but supporters will need to help pony up for those expenses. 

The Boston Globe's shrinking of staff and coverage of local meetings and events has not got the job done for the metropolitan towns. But it's trying, too. Freedom of the press costs money, but it's essential to freedom of its citizens.

comments.body: I was fortunate to be able to attend opening night in Edinburgh. It is hard to describe how magnificent and impactful this opera is. The music, words and staging all combined to draw me towards the magnificent life-sized horses in the first act (who wouldn't want to touch their glossy coats?) and recoil in horror, while still mesmerized, at the cost of riding them in the second act. It is probably not lost on anyone that "horse" is a synonym for heroin in the drug world - but no explanation is needed.  I have never experienced opera like this. It is now, it is real, it is tragedy as it exists today.  Congratulations to all for this creative masterpiece and for the courage to address this issue with such frank and unsettling honesty. comments.name: Joe Pearce
comments.body:
My God, does this nonsense never end? How many opera lovers or opera-goers (not always exactly the same thing) really want to visit the local noise pit at $100 or more a throw to hear an opera about the opioid crisis? Really? No doubt Mr. Gelb's social conscience will dictate that it should be put on here, but maybe an attack of overriding financial intelligence will prevail. 

I'm sorry that Ms. Mazzoli and her librettist have lost relatives and/or friends due to the opioid crisis, but to use it as an excuse to write an opera on a decidedly unpalatable subject smacks almost of license. On the paternal side of my family, I've last a father, a grandfather, three aunts, an uncle and at least four cousins to cancer, yet I have never felt I should be writing a play or opera libretto on Galloping Cancer. It wouild certainly be a tragic one. But I might counter it by writing one of the maternal side of my family, where there is no cancer, but only a kind of  creeping idiocy. That might make a good comic opera. Perhaps I could combine them - a kind of Amfortas-meets-Dulcamara scenario. Yes, i really must get this onto the opera stage before I croak. Hey, everybody else is doing it and I want my chance at temporary immortality!

Conflating the legacy of the Sackler family name to the generosity of one branch of the family (arts patronage) with the other branch of the family (maximizing profit from pain killers) should be avoided. This was explained in a relatively recent NYT obituary of a member of the Sackler family. 
The impact of pain medicine addiction on society and families is horrendous and ethically wrong. 
Kudos to M Mazzoli and others for creating music to address this harsh and painful reality ! Mazzoli’s prior compositions have been performed by the Cincinnati symphony orchestra. Looking forward to hearing more of her musical voice!

comments.name: Alexander Bain
comments.body:
A Google Books search found an earlier instance of "Galloping Cure", in Cosmopolitan in late 1963, in the headline of a short piece on the then-trendy "d-lysergic acid diethylamide tartrate, a supposedly non-addictive drug". Now known as LSD.

Kudos to the librettist and composer for resurrecting this apt phrase. If tickets aren't already sold out I would like to travel to SF to experience the opera. Since the early 1960s our mortality rate due to illegal drugs has gone up by a factor of 10 and is now roughly the same as our mortality rate from alcohol, which has merely doubled. It is a sad reflection of our way of life that we do so little about this, other than performative but useless exercises like blowing up suspected drug boats. If opera can help turn this around even a little bit, it will be a better use of my hard-earned money than my tax dollars being wasted by the DEA.

comments.body:
The folks going to such lengths want to be parents - whereas probably a high percentage of us did not arrive here through such intention. 

As someone who experienced infertility, I too heard the chorus of “ just adopt” from well meaning folks who themselves had never been through either scenario. Adopting is not an easy or inexpensive process for all involved - not the mothers in impossible situations, the kids, or the adoptive parents. The other common route is through foster care, but the ultimate goal is for family reunification, which is in the interest of the child. Of course it doesn’t always happen and bless the angels who are able to step in and provide love and care, though that’s not always the case either. 

Someone choosing to be a parent is the best case scenario - but even then genetics are a crapshoot and one has to be willing to parent the kid they get. 

Make the world better for kids and families no matter the configuration and it’d be a boon for society. We need more than the nuclear family anyways.

comments.name: Walter Goodman
comments.body: The “no such thing as a free lunch” problem is daunting and insurmountable. Medicare beneficiaries have significant deductibles, premiums and co-insurance which is why half of them opt for Medicare Advantage and so many others buy supplemental plans. Eliminating the cost-sharing would cause an explosion of demand, which raises the other major problem with “Medicare for All” which is the inadequacy of Medicare provider rates. With a few exceptions, Medicare pays physicians and hospitals at rates that fall below the average cost of care (and the resulting cost shift is a significant factor in high commercial insurance premiums) but above the marginal cost. And, if you lose $1 on every unit, you can’t make it up by increasing volume. Impose Medicare payment rates for all services and the high fixed cost health care delivery system will implode. When queried about this, Bernie Sanders (who’s never met a payroll in his life) says, they’ll have to be “more efficient” but that’s delusional.

Does the price fall when the quality does? These last two reviews—Marcel and Bistro Ha—make plain your take on dining in New York, a take that’s been there the whole time but not so clearly. We should look for and value small, scrappy (newyorkie), young, ambitious places with food that we might not have encountered before. We should avoid large, well-healed, older, places (ambitious or not), with food that we are probably familiar with.  In the first case, we should overlook flaws. In the second, we absolutely should not. As a program, it’s understandable. It may even be admirable. For a lot of potential diners (diners, not just readers) it’s an odd guide, especially with prices what they are. You love expensive tasting menus, but that’s not realistic for everyone. I, personally, wish you could find more “solid” and “dependable,” and “very good,” even if they’re less exciting. Something I can count on, not gamble on.

Marginalia comes from Latin ‘margo’ meaning ‘border, brink, or edge’, and -alia’ a plural suffix meaning ‘things relating to’ or ‘collection of.’

Compare with scholium.

comments.name: Charles Kaufmann
comments.body: I had a similar experience in 2012 with my Longfellow Chorus and Orchestra performing unpublished works by Samuel Coleridge-Taylor (1875–1912). This was before the SC-T renaissance; none of my professional musicians had heard of him. I had programmed SC-T's major work, "Scenes From the Song of Hiawatha," to correspond with the centennial of his death. On June 5, 2012, I wanted to recreate the June 5, 1912, premiere of his Violin Concerto by Maud Powell at what is now the Yale Norfolk Festival. The concerto was too long. But I found the unpublished concert piece Powell played as an encore, "Keep Me From Sinking Down." The manuscript was in the Royal Conservatory of Music library. SC-T's handwriting in letters is almost unreadable. His music manuscript is clear and exacting. I transcribed parts for my orchestra. Almost exactly 100 years later, day and time, we performed the encore on the same stage in Norfolk where Maud Powell played it. The orchestra accompanying Powell was made up of NY Phil musicians, whose conductor had recently been Mahler. It was as if Maud Powell and SC-T were present with us. It was one of SC-T's last works. He died suddenly three months later at the age of 37. This was not the only SC-T manuscript I transcribed: the Violin Concerto, "Overture to Hiawatha," several of his arrangements of "24 Negro Melodies" for piano. I tell this story in my feature documentary, "Samuel Coleridge-Taylor and His Music in America, 1900–1912." https://youtu.be/HebDy-sLdCs

With so little information, how can random visa cancellations be tracked or explained?

Every summer for many decades our elderly Australian friend came to NYC to visit his daughter, an American citizen, and then to go to Europe for the tennis, see some theater in London, before returning to NYC where we would all celebrate his birthday.

Last summer he came to NYC as usual, went to Europe as usual, but the day before his flight from London to NYC he was notified that his visa waiver was cancelled and he would be denied entry to the US. 
No explanation, no appeal.

He lost his London-NYC ticket and his NYC-Sydney ticket and had to buy a last minute London-Sydney ticket.
And we had to cancel his 94th birthday party. 
He's not coming this year for his 95th birthday, can't risk it. 

If you are issued a visa (on in the case of Australians, a visa waiver) but it can be cancelled at any time, even mid-trip, without explanation, who can travel in reliance on one?
